summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of type 2 diabetes, psoriatic arthritis on chronic steroids, adrenal insufficiency, and prior pulmonary embolism was admitted for evaluation of redness and swelling in the left leg. Initially concerning for cellulitis, the presentation improved rapidly without antibiotics, and findings were attributed to bilateral lower extremity edema with dependent rubor due to fluid overload, following a 20-pound weight gain. He was treated with intravenous furosemide, achieving 4 liters of net diuresis over two days. His INR was subtherapeutic at 1.7 on admission, prompting an additional 2 mg warfarin dose; it improved to 2.1 by discharge. A new left thumb paronychia was diagnosed on hospital day two and managed with warm soaks and mupirocin ointment. Despite initial plans to adjust diuretics, the patient was discharged on his prior regimen of furosemide, bumetanide, and spironolactone with high-dose potassium supplementation, per patient and family preference and outpatient provider coordination. He was stable at discharge with improved edema and weight reduction to 393 pounds.
problems: Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
